extracted.intended_audience: aspiring comedy performers and sketch writers (especially those aiming for SNL/Second City/iO)
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and practical guidelines for creating, adapting, pitching, and producing sketch comedy for venues like Second City, iO, and Saturday Night Live — including submission packet composition, audition/showcase behavior, writing choices (parody, thesis, voice), table-read/production techniques, and career mindset.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing packet composition
rubrics_metrics.description: When submitting a packet I did submit a writing packet. Several over the years, actually. I don't remember what they consisted of, but I'm sure they had 4-5 sketches in them that I thought could be used on the show.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include ~4–5 sketches. Use pieces that have been working best in your two-person sketch shows, solo show pieces, and Second City scenes; adjust parts here or there so they work on paper and not just in performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make performance pieces work on paper
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjust performance pieces so they function on the page and not only in live performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take the pieces that worked in live shows and modify them (change a part here or there) to translate to a written packet; SNL reads packets on paper, so ensure jokes and beats are clear without physical performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Showcase and audition visibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Lorne Michaels, Seth Meyers, and a group of producers and writers from SNL came out and watched me do showcases at iO and shows at Second City over the years. I was flown out to NYC to do a 5-minute audition at SNL in both 2005 and 2009.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform regularly at notable improv/sketch houses (Second City, iO) and do showcases; be prepared for short auditions (e.g., 5 minutes). Visibility in live showcases can lead to callbacks/hiring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor material to the show's style
rubrics_metrics.description: You learn quickly what doesn't work on the show and more slowly what should instead be pitched. Soon, I could just look at my notes and be like, that's an idea that might work if I performed it alone in Chicago, but just doesn't fit what we do here.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand the target show's tone, format, and audience expectations; don't assume material that works locally will fit a national sketch show—edit or discard ideas that aren't a match.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make parodies accessible to unfamiliar audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: It was an interesting challenge right off the bat because we were parodying something that was not known by many of our viewers, so we tried to make it funny on its own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When parodying niche or obscure source material, craft the sketch so its humor stands alone; provide enough context or relatable framing (e.g., the universal frustrations of outdoor festivals) so viewers who don't know the source can still laugh.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heighten beyond the source material
rubrics_metrics.description: You have to try to make it even crazier than a pretty wild source video.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Escalate elements of the source to make the parody punchier and clearer; aim to amplify the absurdity so it reads as intentional satire rather than mere imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mean-spirited/cheap shots
rubrics_metrics.description: I've learned the value of laying off the cheap shot. The size of our audience holds you accountable for what you say, so if you're looking to take someone down, make sure it's not someone who is just doing their own thing and not hurting anyone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful of punching down or attacking individuals gratuitously; prefer targets or premises that are fair game and serve the joke rather than personal cruelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Have a clear thesis/defining line for the scene
rubrics_metrics.description: The next challenges were making sure we don't unfairly attack Smashmouth ... The final touches that helped get it to air were Seth coming in with the line that defines our thesis statement: 'I would sing it for you, but I don't want it to get stuck in your head, too'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify a central idea or line that defines the scene's point of view; a strong thesis line can crystallize the joke and guide performance choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use staging and camera techniques for surprise
rubrics_metrics.description: SNL producer Steve Higgins helping us figure out the best way to keep startling the audience by teaching the camera techniques we could use to mislead the viewer and surprise them with another Smashmouth entrance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Think visually and collaborate with production: use camera angles, blocking, and misdirection to create repeated surprises and maximize laughs, not just rely on dialogue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage table reads for timing and delivery
rubrics_metrics.description: The table read was probably my favorite part of that week because Ms. White has obviously been a part of so many table reads in her life that she put on a clinic in timing and delivery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use table reads to refine pacing, timing, and delivery; experienced actors' instincts can teach you how lines land and where beats need to change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Get production out of people through confident kindness
rubrics_metrics.description: From watching Seth I've learned that you get better production out of your fellow comedians through confident kindness than through any intimidation or punishments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lead writers/performers with clear, confident direction delivered kindly to get better performances and a more collaborative environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop a gut sense for when material has lost an audience
rubrics_metrics.description: You start to get a gut feeling after tons of table read scenes ... when you can feel that one has just lost its audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate intuition through repeated table reads and production experience to recognize scenes that drag or have lost their comedic momentum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve and cultivate your unique voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Everything I've ever gotten has come to me when I stopped trying to get things, and focused on finding and performing in my own voice. ... finding a way to write things that are truly in my voice and have something about them that feels like my favorite scenes I saw or did in Chicago ... and to make those work on a nationally televised TV show.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spend the bulk of your time on projects that are truly unique to you and excite you; aim to translate your personal voice into formats that reach wider audiences without losing its distinctiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't be married to one career path; set healthy goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't get married to one path. I see a lot of people who let the fact that Second City or SNL has not hired them cause them to become bitter and/or quit comedy. I think it's healthier to set goals like, 'I want to be working with friends and producing interesting comedy for a living some time soon,' than 'I need to get Second City main stage by 2012 and SNL by 2015 or I've failed.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain flexibility in career planning; set process- and lifestyle-oriented goals rather than rigid milestone deadlines to avoid bitterness and burnout.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't waste energy comparing yourself to others
rubrics_metrics.description: Lastly, don't spend any energy worrying about what other comedians have been hired for, whether they deserve it, whether their last joke was good or not... Just worry about your own stuff and do your best to enjoy all the hilarious people out there without judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on developing your own material and craft; avoid unproductive comparisons that distract from creative work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cast and write to performers' strengths
rubrics_metrics.description: Colin and I were also excited about how Jason played DJ Supersoak. His look was loosely based on DJ Clay, but he's really just doing an original, energetic Sudeikis character that cracked us up. Same with Nasim. Lil Blaster was a different vibe from other stuff she did on the show and she was absolutely hilarious at it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, tailor characters and beats to the unique comedic strengths of the performers who will play them; an actor's persona can elevate material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground parodies in relatable, shared experiences
rubrics_metrics.description: The fact is, in the past 10 years I've become way less into all-day outdoor concert events and the video is making that statement as much as it's parodying the ICP infomercial. There's never any bathrooms, you're sunburned, you haven't heard of half the bands... Hopefully anyone who's been to Lollapalooza, Warped, etc will relate to this fictional festival that is the worst of all those things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anchor parodies in universal or widely shared experiences so that even viewers unfamiliar with the specific target can relate and find humor in the situation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do research on real people or subjects you parody
rubrics_metrics.description: The next challenges were making sure we don't unfairly attack Smashmouth who I don't know personally, but all our research pointed to them being really good guys.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate the real people or groups you're satirizing to avoid unfair, inaccurate, or harmful portrayals; research can inform tone and keep satire from feeling mean-spirited.
